title: The remains of a star gone supernova
caption: The supernova remnant SNR 0519, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: SNR B0519-69.0 · constellation Dorado · about 150000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Thin, blood-red shells made of delicate wisps of gas curve through this Hubble image. Together they form SNR B0519-69.0, usually shortened to SNR 0519, the debris of a star whose supernova explosion happened around 600 years ago.

There are several kinds of supernova. In this case, astronomers know the exploding star was a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a Sun-like star in the last stage of its life. The unstable star exploded violently, and these thin shells are what remains.

SNR 0519 lies more than 150,000 light-years away in the southern constellation Dorado, the Dolphinfish. That constellation also holds most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, so this part of the sky is crowded with interesting deep-sky objects. The remnant sits within that neighboring galaxy.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.33 x 1.62 arcminutes) and distance (150000 light years), the frame spans roughly 145 × 71 light-years. Its light set out about 150,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the remnant through a visual filter and a filter near the hydrogen-alpha line. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The thin shells glow faintly in hydrogen light and would be invisible to the eye at this distance.

behind.people: See full credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA. Acknowledgement: Claude Cornen
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud is the fourth largest galaxy in our Local Group. Hubble has seen a similar remnant there, SNR B0509-67.5, which came from the same type of supernova and looks very similar. Claude Cornen's version of this image won sixth prize in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition.
alt: Thin, delicate red shells of gas from an exploded star.
